Fluctuations of the second $\sigma$ field affect the duration of inflation and therefore the curvature perturbation of the universe at reheating. If the relationship between $\sigma$ and $\zeta$ is non-linear, then non-Gaussianities of the local kind are produced.
\small Contour plot for the parameters of the EFT Lagrangian $c_s$ and $\tilde c_3$ from WMAP7yr. Figure takes from~\cite{Senatore:2009gt}.
\small Contour plots of parameters of the EFT of Inflation Lagrangian from the Planck team~\cite{Ade:2013ydc,Ade:2015ava}. Figure from~\cite{Ade:2015ava}.

\small As the slow roll parameter becomes smaller and smaller, the spacetime during inflation becomes more and more unperturbed, and the one after inflation more and more perturbed. The surface of constant $\phi=\phi_{\rm reheating}$, in red, becomes more and more perturbed, curved, reaching infinite volume  with a non-zero probability in the eternal regime. Figure from~\cite{Creminelli:2008es}.

\small Typical shape for the probability distribution of the volume $\rho(V)$. For small volumes the behavior is gaussian with the number of $e$-foldings ($\rho\sim e^{-c(N-\overline N)^2}$); for volumes larger than the average value $\overline V$, $\rho(V)$ follows a power law in the volume ($\rho\sim 1/V^\alpha$) that eventually turns into an exponential law ($\rho \sim e^{-{\rm const}\cdot V}$) at large enough volumes ($V\gtrsim V_b$, with $V_b$ representing the classical volume obtained if the inflation started from a barrier at the top of the potential). When $\epsilon<\epsilon_c$ the exponential tail starts earlier at $V\simeq V_\epsilon=e^{\pi/(2\sqrt{1-\Omega})}$ and the integral of the probability distribution for finite volumes becomes smaller than one. The average volume is $\bar V={\rm Exp}\left[\tfrac{2 N_{\rm cl}}{1+\sqrt{1-\Omega^{-1}}}\right]$. We see that as $\Omega$ starts very large in standard inflation and approaches the phase transition, the average volume interpolates between Exp$[3N_{\rm cl}]$ to Exp$[6N_{\rm cl}]$. Figure from~\cite{Dubovsky:2008rf}.

\small A potential with an absolute minimum and a de Sitter local minimum. If the inflaton happens to be in the false vacuum and the tunnelling rate is sufficiently small, this situation leads to false vacuum eternal inflation.

\small A representation of a region of universe that is undergoing false vacuum eternal inflation. Bubbles that nucleated earlier have had more time to expand, but as time goes on, the volume of the false vacuum grows as well. Figure from~\cite{Kleban:2011pg}.

abstracts.value: In 1980 and the following years, the study of the early universe created the idea of an exponential expansion or quasi-de Sitter stage to solve some cosmological paradoxa. This concept proved to be valuable not only as a modification of the big-bang singularity, but it became fruitful in astrophysical applications as the observation of microwave background inhomogeneities and in cosmic large-scale galaxy structures. The author presents a modern view on the present evolution of these ideas. He describes the development in five lectures, beginning with the exposure of the homogeneity, isotropy and inhomogeneity problem of the classical Friedmann-Robertson-Walker models in lecture 1. The exposition in this part is sometimes a bit loosely, with many inaccuracies in the formulae. However, the introduction of the scalar field dynamics and the smallness parameters describing the inflationary stage are intuitively compelling explained.Lecture 2 is then devoted to the generation of inhomogeneities resulting from quantum fluctuations and their stretching to macroscopic scales during the exponential expansion. Lecture 3 is devoted to observational effects of scalar and tensor perturbations, mainly on the microwave anisotropies, but the author also develops an effective field theory of inflation beyond the slow motion approximation. In Lecture 4, the author presents his own research results on the statistical characterization of the generated perturbation with an transparent and readable exposition of the intricate calculations leading to perturbations with non-Gaussianity statistics. These result in measurable effects in microwave anisotropies that are strongly restricted by recent experiments. The final lecture presents the idea of an eternal inflation as an effect of quantum gravity in the early universe, that gives rise to speculations of multiverses as alternatives to the classical big-bang picture.The exposition is well suited to all people that are interested in fundamental relations between quantum physics and gravitation theory, and to all scholars of the early universe. It contains a lot of basic formulas for the beginning of such studies, however sometimes with inaccuracies and misprints. In the further exposition the way to complex calculations are nicely conveyed.
